Optimizing Spinach Growth in Simulated Lunar Conditions: Investigating Soil
Composition and Nutrient Amendments for Extraterrestrial Agriculture
Team Name: OCSA Green Technology Club
Team ID: 19034
Ryan Jung, Andrew Jung, Henry Kim, Aryan Sharma, Isaac Chun
Challenge category: High School

Introduction
Like all other living organims, plants have definite needs for their growth and cultivation. Plants
grow and develop mainly through photosynthesis, transforming light energy into chemical
energy stored in glucose—a very important compound that serves to fuel their growth. To do
this, plants require a sufficient supply of light, water, air, and essential nutrients from the soil. All
these elements are critical in driving photosynthesis, supporting the development of a strong root
system, and generally maintaining the health of plants (Johnson, 2016). Additionally,
environmental factors like temperature and soil pH influence plant growth, and interactions with
beneficial microorganisms can increase nutrient uptake and tolerance.
More recent milestones, such as NASA's Artemis program and international lunar exploration
initiatives, have sparked a new era of sustained presence on the Moon, making plant cultivation
in space one of the most critical research areas. Plants provide reliable sustenance and contribute
significantly to producing oxygen and recycling carbon dioxide, which is indispensable in
long-duration space travel. However, because of the harsh lunar conditions and lack of earthy
soil, new agricultural methods must be designed for growing and sustaining on the Moon.
The moon's surface is blanketed by lunar regolith, a layer of loose, fragmental, rocky material. In
contrast to terrestrial soil, regolith lacks organic matter on which microbial life and nutrient
cycling could be supported. It also lacks nutrients essential to plant growth, including nitrogen
and phosphorus. Moreover, lunar regolith has a sharp and abrasive texture, a low capacity for
water retention, and a high pH, which can impede traditional agricultural practices (Ding et al.,
2024).
The experiment described herein will help answer such challenges by investigating spinach
plants' growth in various terrestrial soil mixtures and lunar regolith simulants. It would aim to
explore the optimal plant growth medium in a lunar environment with nutritional amendments
like nitrogen and phosphorus and mixtures of Earth soil with regolith simulant. The results will
facilitate progress in current lunar farming research.
Research Question:
How does soil composition, either 50% Earth soil and 50% lunar simulant versus 100% lunar
simulant with nutrient amendments such as phosphorus and nitrogen, or both combined, affect
spinach growth in a simulated lunar environment?

Controls: Red Growth Light (12hr on/off), temperature range (indoor), humidity, and watering
(using soil moisture meter) will be kept constant across all groups to ensure that observed
differences are solely due to soil and nutrient conditions.
Rationale for Parameter:
Research in lunar agriculture shows that it is difficult for plants to grow in pure regolith due to
low nutrients, absence of organic matter, and problems related to water retention (Fackrell et al.,
2024). Lunar soil has low cation exchange capacity (CEC) that makes retaining nutrients very
difficult for plants (Jackson & Saha, 2024). Most studies have shown nutrient supplementation to
be very crucial for plants in lunar environment, since regolith does not hold nutrients and
retention like Earth soil does. Adding micronutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus and adjusting
soil composition aims to remedy these deficiencies for healthy growth by potentially satisfying
plant’s nutrition requirements and improving water retention.
Experimental design:
To begin the experiment, soil mixtures will be prepared by thoroughly mixing Earth soil and
lunar simulant in appropriate ratios using percent conversion of volumes. In preparing the 50%
Earth soil and 50% lunar simulant composition, equal portions of each material will be measured
and mixed until the blend appears uniform. Only lunar simulant will be used for the 100% lunar
simulant composition. Each pot will be filled with 200 mL of corresponding soil composition. It
will be ensured that the soil mix in all pots is packed well and distributed evenly to form an
adequate control across the experimental groups.
Once the soil is prepared, micronutrients will be applied to each pot. With 1.5g of phosphorus
granules incorporated into the soil, those plants are labeled as phosphorus following the nutrient
amendment schedule. Pots receiving the combination of phosphorus and nitrogen will be given
0.75g of each. In the nitrogen-only treatment, 1.5g of nitrogen granules will be applied.
Micronutrient application will be uniform over the soil in each pot to prevent any localized
concentration. Additionally, control group would not receive any amendments.

Spinach seeds, chosen for its fast rate of germination and growth, will be planted in each pot.
Three seeds will be sown evenly and about ¼ inch in depth into the soil. This will provide a
proper and uniform condition of germination and growth. Then, pots are placed in an
environment whose main variables, such as temperature, humidity, and light, remain constant
throughout the experiment.
Lighting will be in the form of 12-hour cycles of red light in a growth chamber, imitating equal
conditions in moisture, temperature, and alternate factors for photosynthesis.
The watering will be on a daily basis (omitted if sufficient water level), depending on our sensor
monitors' soil moisture. Drip irrigation is used in maintaining soil moisture at a 50% constant
level and ensuring there is uniformity of moisture in the soil for the plants. Every plant is
watered with just the right amount, which comes out uniformly via the irrigation system. So, the
moisture of the soil will be monitored by a soil moisture meter and accordingly, adjustments will
be made to maintain the optimum growing conditions. All the watering during the experiment
shall be done with distilled water to ensure that no unaccounted minerals or chemicals are added.
Measurement & procedure:
Data will be collected every three days over the eight-week experimental period. Measurements
will include plant height, leaf count (data not shown due to space limitations), and stem diameter
to assess growth and development. The environmental data, including temperature, humidity, and
soil moisture, are also accounted for. Finally, plants will be harvested at the end of the
experiment to measure additional metrics that quantify biomass and photosynthetic capacity,
such as shoot dry weight. Digital photographs will also be taken periodically over time to
visually represent the progress and development of plants.

Discussion
The experimental results revealed that spinach plants achieved optimal growth in the 50% Earth
soil + 50% lunar regolith mixture supplemented with both phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N)
amendments. This group consistently exhibited the greatest plant height, dry mass, and overall
health, underscoring the importance of balanced nutrient supplementation and soil composition
in extraterrestrial farming. In contrast, the 100% lunar regolith groups demonstrated significantly
reduced growth, highlighting the challenges associated with using lunar regolith as a standalone
growth medium due to its low nutrient content, poor water retention, and high alkalinity.
Plant Height ( Figure 2.1)
The tallest plants grew in the 50% Earth + 50% Lunar soil mixture with a combination of
phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N). This can be explained by the role of these nutrients in plant
physiology:

Nitrogen's Role Nitrogen is a critical macronutrient for plant growth. It is a key
component of amino acids, proteins, and chlorophyll. Chlorophyll directly impacts
photosynthesis, enabling plants to produce the energy needed for growth. Nitrogen
deficiency has been linked to stunted growth and pale leaves due to reduced chlorophyll
content (Zayed et al., 2023).
Phosphorus's Role Phosphorus is essential for energy transfer within the plant, as it is a
primary component of ATP (adenosine triphosphate). It supports root development and
early plant growth (Khan et al., 2023).
Synergistic Nutrient Effects The combination of phosphorus and nitrogen increases
photosynthesis and metabolic processes compared to using a single nutrient, increasing
growth. This is consistent with results from terrestrial agriculture, where balanced
nutrient management has been shown to increase crop yield substantially than single
nutrient (Tilman et al., 2002).
Soil Composition Impact The 50% Earth + 50% Lunar mixture provided a more
favorable physical environment than pure lunar simulant. Terrestrial soil likely
contributed organic matter and improved the medium's water retention and aeration
properties.
Soil pH (Figure 2.2)
All soils started at a high pH of 8.0 but stabilized at 7.0 over the 8 weeks.
High Initial pH in Lunar Regolith: Lunar regolith is inherently alkaline due to its
mineralogical composition (Ding et al., 2024). These compounds dissolve in water,
creating an initial high pH environment unsuitable for plant growth.
pH Stabilization: The decrease in pH over time could be attributed to nutrient
amendments and organic acids released during plant root exudation. For instance,
phosphorus fertilizers can react with soil components, slightly reducing pH. Additionally,
root exudates, including organic acids like citric acid, are known to acidify the
rhizosphere, promoting nutrient solubility (Ma et al., 2022).
3. Figure 2.3: Soil Moisture
The higher water retention in the 50% Earth + 50% Lunar soil mixture compared to pure lunar
simulant is consistent with the properties of terrestrial soil:

Terrestrial Soil Contribution: Earth soil contains organic matter and clay particles,
which improve water-holding capacity due to their high surface area and hydrophilic
properties (UNL, n.d.). Lunar regolith, by contrast, lacks organic matter and has a coarse,
abrasive texture, resulting in poor water retention.
Impact of Nutrient Amendments: Soils with phosphorus and nitrogen amendments
retained more moisture. This could be due to fertilizers improving soil aggregation and
structure, indirectly enhancing water-holding capacity (Khangura et al., 2023).
4. Figure 2.4: Final Shoot Dry Mass
The dry mass data corroborates the plant height results. The P + N treatment consistently
supported optimal growth and biomass production.
Macronutrient in Lunar environment: The final shoot dry mass results align with the
plant height data (Figure 2.1), demonstrating that the combination of phosphorus (P) and
nitrogen (N) amendments consistently supported the highest levels of growth and
biomass production across all soil compositions. These findings highlight the critical role
of macronutrient availability in enhancing plant physiological processes, particularly in
resource-limited environments like those simulated with lunar regolith.
Assumptions and Limitations The experiment assumed that nutrient amendments and soil
mixtures would have uniform effects across all plants. Environmental conditions such as
temperature, light, and humidity were also controlled but could have been more extensively
optimized or varied to simulate potential fluctuations in lunar environments. Another assumption
was that the lunar simulant accurately represented lunar regolith, though particle size and
chemical composition differences may exist.
Future Improvements To enhance the experiment, future iterations should:
1. Investigate the effects of varying light spectrums and intensities to better replicate lunar
lighting conditions.
2. Include more granular monitoring of soil pH and nutrient depletion over time to refine
amendment strategies.
3. Test additional soil mixtures and alternative amendments to identify other viable options
for plant growth.
4. Expand the scope to include longer growth cycles and the effects of recycling plant
material to simulate a closed-loop system.

This study provides a solid foundation for future research into extraterrestrial agriculture,
advancing the development of sustainable food production systems for long-term space missions
and lunar habitation.
Conclusion:
This experiment shows that it is possible to improve plant growth in extraterrestrial
environments through adjustings soil composition and targeted nutrient amendments. The results
bring into light the critical importance of soil composition, nutrient balance, and water retention
in optimizing plant development in challenging conditions. The 50% Earth soil + 50% lunar
regolith mixture, enriched with phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N), was found to consistently
provide the best environment for spinach growth with the highest plant height, biomass, and
overall health of the plants compared to the other treatments.
These findings show that crops can be grown on the Moon using appropriate soil amendments
and mixtures. Such a study will also provide valuable insights into the physiological
requirements of plants under resource-limited settings and opens avenues toward innovative
solutions in extraterrestrial agriculture. This research contributes to the bigger goal of sustaining
human life during long-term space exploration missions by addressing the challenges of lunar
regolith. The pace of future research in light optimization, nutrient cycling, and alternative soil
amendments will only fine-tune these strategies, furthering by degrees humanity's ability to grow
food away from Earth.
